name: Robert Louis Stevenson
note: THE ROOM HOLDS TREASURE ISLAND ENTIRE, AND THE MAP IT CAME FROM. In the late summer of 1881, kept indoors by rain at Braemar, Stevenson drew and coloured a map of an island to amuse his schoolboy stepson, Lloyd Osbourne, and wrote 'Treasure Island' in the corner. The story grew out of the map, a chapter a day read aloud to the family after lunch. The way in is his own account of that, 'My First Book', written the year he died; then the verses he set before the novel; then the thirty-four chapters, split by chapter and unedited — they are also what the Amenti Studios cutter reads. One other passage stands beside them: Henry Jekyll's full statement, the other face of the same writer, the one who could not stop at boys' adventure. Everything in this room is public domain.

works.section: Essays in the Art of Writing (1905)
works.title: My First Book: Treasure Island
works.source: Robert Louis Stevenson, “My First Book: Treasure Island”, The Idler, August 1894; collected in Essays in the Art of Writing (1905) · Project Gutenberg #492 · public domain
works.note: The map, the rain at Braemar, the schoolboy stepson it was drawn for, the chapters read aloud day by day after lunch, his father joining in to draw up the inventory of Billy Bones's chest — and the map itself lost on the way to the publishers, so that he had to draw it again from the finished book, working out the island from the story instead of the story from the island. Written in Samoa in the last year of his life.

works.note: The verses and the dedication he set before the novel: 'If sailor tales to sailor tunes, / Storm and adventure, heat and cold…' — and the book dedicated to S.L.O., Samuel Lloyd Osbourne, 'an American gentleman in accordance with whose classic taste the following narrative has been designed.'
